analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to speed up, standardize, and publicly report their prior-authorization decisions.
analysis.headline: A bill to speed up Medicare Advantage care approvals drew 59 Senate cosponsors from both parties, but died in the Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: About half of Medicare beneficiaries are in Medicare Advantage, private plans that often require doctors to get advance approval — "prior authorization" — before delivering care, and delays or denials can postpone treatment. This bill would require plans that use prior authorization to adopt a standardized electronic approval system, report to the government and publish how many requests they approve or deny (including decisions made with artificial intelligence), give enrollees and doctors access to the criteria used, and let the Health and Human Services Secretary set response deadlines as short as 24 hours. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, roughly half of Medicare beneficiaries, who currently face approval delays and denials for items and services like post-acute care and imaging. Doctors and hospitals also gain from less paperwork and faster answers, and high-performing providers could get exemptions from prior authorization entirely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage enrollees and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Advantage plans that use prior authorization would have to run a standardized electronic system for submitting and answering requests, explicitly excluding fax machines and proprietary portals that don't meet federal standards, starting with plan years in 2027.

Plans would have to report annually — and the government would publish plan-by-plan on a public CMS website — the percentage and number of requests approved and denied, how often denials were appealed and overturned, how long decisions took, and whether artificial intelligence or automated tools were used to make the decisions.

Enrollees could request the criteria a plan uses to decide prior authorization requests, and providers would get access to those criteria and an itemized list of required documentation before signing contracts.

Plans would have to adopt enrollee-protection standards, including waiving or loosening prior authorization for providers who consistently follow the rules, and reviewing annually which services actually need prior authorization based on their own data.

The Health and Human Services Secretary could set enforceable timeframes for plan responses — such as 24 hours — for expedited requests, routinely approved services, and other prior authorization requests, on top of the existing 72-hour rule.

MedPAC and the Government Accountability Office would study how prior authorization is used and how often denied decisions are overturned, and CMS would report on how to create real-time approvals for routinely approved services.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers bear the cost of building electronic prior authorization systems, compiling detailed annual denial and appeal data, and facing public exposure of their denial rates and use of AI in deciding care. Some of that cost could be passed to beneficiaries through premiums or benefit design, and insurers argue prior authorization is a tool for holding down premiums and screening out unnecessary care.

drawbacks.text: The bill places new technology and reporting requirements on Medicare Advantage insurers, and compliance costs could be recovered through higher premiums or slimmer benefits rather than absorbed by company margins.

Prior authorization exists partly to hold down premiums and catch unnecessary or risky care; a faster, more automatic approval system could weaken that check if poorly calibrated, which is why the bill builds in provider performance standards and annual reviews rather than banning prior authorization.

The bill relies heavily on later rulemaking by the Secretary and requires reports to Congress years out — a GAO evaluation not due until 2032 — so even if enacted, its real-world effect would depend on how future administrations write and enforce the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete: faster answers for seniors waiting on care, public data showing which plans deny the most requests, and limits on opaque AI-driven denials. The costs are real but modest relative to the stakes — compliance spending by insurers and some risk that weakened utilization review nudges premiums up. The bill is not radical: it does not ban prior authorization, it standardizes and illuminates it, and it lets high-performing doctors escape it. The honest criticism is that transparency takes years to translate into enforcement, and the long timeline of reports and rulemaking means seniors would feel the effects slowly even if it had passed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, sat there with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill in the Senate on June 13, 2024, with 44 original cosponsors listed from both parties.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day of introduction, which was the only action it ever received.

By the end, the bill had 59 cosponsors: 32 of 48 Senate Democrats, 26 of 49 Senate Republicans, and 1 of the 4 Independents — a majority of the Senate signed on, split almost evenly between the parties.

The Finance Committee never scheduled a hearing or a vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing it under the rule that bills die when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers came out ahead: no new electronic prior-authorization mandate, no public reporting of denial and appeal rates, no AI-disclosure requirements, and no federally set response deadlines. Seniors in Medicare Advantage continue under the prior-authorization rules that existed before the bill, with no added transparency about denials.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost evenly split across party lines — 32 of 48 Senate Democrats, 26 of 49 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 4 Independents cosponsored — and no senator is recorded as opposing it; the bill died in committee, not on the floor.

industries.note: Prior authorization is these insurers' main tool for managing utilization and costs, and the bill would force them to move approvals onto standardized electronic systems, disclose denial and appeal rates publicly, and reveal when AI makes the decisions. Insurers argue the requirements protect plan value; patients experience the other side of that tool as delayed or denied care, so the industry's interest in keeping it unrestrained runs against seniors' access in this bill — though the electronic mandate itself would trim some administrative cost.

Providers would get standardized electronic submissions, faster response deadlines, access to plans' approval criteria, and possible waiver of prior authorization for high performers — less paperwork and fewer treatment delays for their Medicare Advantage patients.
The mandate for standards-based electronic prior authorization would create demand for systems that transmit requests, documentation, and responses between providers and plans.
